claim: Mitral cells and tufted cells exhibit distinct activity in vivo.
source: While long viewed as essentially equivalent neuron classes, emerging evidence shows that MCs and TCs exhibit distinct activity in vivo (Nagayama et al., 2004; Fukunaga et al., 2012; Igarashi et al., 2012; Adam et al., 2014; Otazu et al., 2015), suggesting that MCs and TCs encode complementary aspects of olfactory information.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating distinct in vivo activity patterns

claim: Tufted cells respond to lower odor concentrations than mitral cells.
source: For instance, TCs respond to lower odor concentrations than MCs (Igarashi et al., 2012; Kikuta et al., 2013), suggesting that TCs are involved in processing near-threshold stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on concentration-dependent responses

claim: Mitral cells and tufted cells project their axons to many non-overlapping regions.
source: Consistent with this notion of parallel pathways, MCs and TCs project their axons to many non-overlapping regions (Nagayama et al., 2010; Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies

claim: Tufted cells are more intrinsically excitable than mitral cells.
source: For instance, TCs are more intrinsically excitable and receive stronger OSN-mediated excitation than MCs (Gire et al., 2012; Burton and Urban, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies

claim: Tufted cells receive stronger OSN-mediated excitation than mitral cells.
source: For instance, TCs are more intrinsically excitable and receive stronger OSN-mediated excitation than MCs (Gire et al., 2012; Burton and Urban, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies

claim: Lateral inhibitory circuits enhance contrast and facilitate discrimination of similar stimuli by decorrelating neural responses throughout the brain.
source: Throughout the brain, lateral inhibitory circuits enhance contrast and facilitate discrimination of similar stimuli by decorrelating neural responses (Hirsch and Gilbert, 1991; Urban, 2002; Gschwend et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on lateral inhibition across brain regions

claim: Lateral inhibition in the olfactory bulb occurs between pairs of mitral cells or tufted cells via reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses with inhibitory granule cells.
source: In the olfactory bulb, lateral inhibition occurs between pairs of MCs or TCs via reciprocal dendrodendritic synapses with inhibitory granule cells (GCs) (Schoppa and Urban, 2003; Egger and Urban, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on olfactory bulb circuitry

claim: Lateral inhibition most strongly affects mitral cells firing at intermediate rates because coincident input is required for the activation of granule cells.
source: Previously, we have shown that lateral inhibition most strongly affects MCs firing at intermediate rates because coincident input is required for the activation of GCs (Arevian et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: Activity-dependent regulation of lateral inhibition strength decorrelates mitral cell responses to similar input more effectively than subtractive or divisive forms of inhibition.
source: This activity-dependent regulation of the strength of lateral inhibition onto MCs decorrelates MC responses to similar input more effectively than subtractive or divisive forms of inhibition (Arevian et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research by the authors

claim: Optogenetic activation of a single M72 glomerulus elicits larger lateral inhibitory currents in nearby mitral cells than in tufted cells.
source: Here, we show that optogenetic activation of a single, gene-targeted glomerulus elicits larger and more asynchronous lateral inhibitory currents in nearby MCs than in TCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Optogenetic activation of a single M72 glomerulus elicits more asynchronous lateral inhibitory currents in nearby mitral cells than in tufted cells.
source: Here, we show that optogenetic activation of a single, gene-targeted glomerulus elicits larger and more asynchronous lateral inhibitory currents in nearby MCs than in TCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Similar proportions of mitral cells (59%) and tufted cells (60%) received lateral inhibitory currents following M72 photostimulation.
source: MCs and TCs showed reliable lateral inhibition following a 10 ms light pulse (Figure 1c,d), and similar proportions of MCs (10/17–59%) and TCs (9/15–60%) received lateral inhibitory currents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing proportions of cells receiving inhibition

claim: The peak amplitude of early inhibition (<250 ms after stimulation) was larger in mitral cells than in tufted cells.
source: The peak amplitude of early inhibition was larger in MCs than in TCs (Figure 1e), while the charge transferred of early phase inhibition was not significantly different (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: The charge transferred of early phase inhibition (<250 ms) was not significantly different between mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: The peak amplitude of early inhibition was larger in MCs than in TCs (Figure 1e), while the charge transferred of early phase inhibition was not significantly different (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f

claim: Both the peak amplitude and charge transferred of late phase inhibition (>250 ms) was significantly larger in mitral cells than in tufted cells.
source: Additionally, both the peak amplitude and charge transferred of late phase inhibition (>250 ms) was significantly larger in MCs than in TCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mitral cells receive a smaller proportion of total inhibition during the early phase than tufted cells.
source: MCs also receive a smaller proportion of total inhibition during the early phase than TCs, indicating that inhibition is more asynchronous onto MCs than onto TCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Granule cells contribute similar proportions of lateral inhibition onto mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: Using this pharmacological approach, we found that GCs contribute similar proportions of lateral inhibition onto MCs and TCs (Figure 1l).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 1l

claim: Glomerular layer circuits make small and uniform contributions to lateral inhibition in mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: These observations indicate that glomerular layer circuits make small and uniform contributions to lateral inhibition in MCs and TCs and thus are not the primary source of differences in lateral inhibition between MCs and TCs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on cells with intact vs. truncated apical dendrites

claim: Glomerular layer circuits are not the primary source of differences in lateral inhibition between mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: These observations indicate that glomerular layer circuits make small and uniform contributions to lateral inhibition in MCs and TCs and thus are not the primary source of differences in lateral inhibition between MCs and TCs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on cells with intact vs. truncated apical dendrites

claim: Similar proportions of mitral cells (64%) and tufted cells (67%) were affected by lateral inhibition in spiking experiments.
source: Similar proportions of MCs (16/25–64%) and TCs (12/18–67%) were affected by lateral inhibition (see Materials and methods), and unaffected cells were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on effects of lateral inhibition on spiking

claim: Mitral cell firing rates were reduced by lateral inhibition selectively when mitral cells fired at intermediate rates (34 ± 11 Hz to 79 ± 22 Hz).
source: For example, the MC in Figure 2b,e was affected by lateral inhibition while firing between 27–76 Hz. Likewise, across a population of 16 MCs, rates between 34 ± 11 Hz and 79 ± 22 Hz were affected by lateral inhibition (Figure 3a–e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Tufted cells were influenced by lateral inhibition only when firing at low rates (10 ± 4 Hz to 43 ± 8 Hz).
source: The example TC in Figure 2c,d,f was affected by lateral inhibition while firing between 5–42 Hz, and across a population of 12 TCs, rates between 10 ± 4 Hz and 43 ± 8 Hz were affected by lateral inhibition (Figure 3a–e, Figure 3—figure supplement 2d–f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Both the lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition were significantly lower in tufted cells than in mitral cells.
source: Both the lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition (i.e. the range of firing rates over which lateral inhibition reduces firing rates) were significantly lower in TCs than in MCs (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e

claim: The average fractional reduction in firing rate was much larger in tufted cells than in mitral cells.
source: The average fractional reduction in firing rate was much larger in TCs than in MCs (Figure 3c), though the absolute firing rate decrease was not significantly different (MC: −8.2 ± 2.5 Hz n = 16, vs TC: −8.8 ± 3.2 Hz n = 12) (Figure 3d,f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The absolute firing rate decrease due to lateral inhibition was not significantly different between mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: The average fractional reduction in firing rate was much larger in TCs than in MCs (Figure 3c), though the absolute firing rate decrease was not significantly different (MC: −8.2 ± 2.5 Hz n = 16, vs TC: −8.8 ± 3.2 Hz n = 12) (Figure 3d,f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Granule cells are subdivided into superficial granule cells (sGCs) and deep granule cells (dGCs) based on morphology.
source: Consistent with MCs and TCs engaging distinct lateral inhibitory circuits within the EPL, classical morphological studies suggest that GCs are subdivided into superficial GCs (sGCs), which innervate the superficial EPL, and deep GCs (dGCs), which innervate the deep EPL (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior morphological studies

claim: Superficial granule cells inhibit tufted cell lateral dendrites in the superficial external plexiform layer.
source: This putative morphological subdivision of GCs suggests that sGCs inhibit TC lateral dendrites in the superficial EPL while dGCs inhibit MC lateral dendrites in the deep EPL (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior morphological studies

claim: Deep granule cells inhibit mitral cell lateral dendrites in the deep external plexiform layer.
source: This putative morphological subdivision of GCs suggests that sGCs inhibit TC lateral dendrites in the superficial EPL while dGCs inhibit MC lateral dendrites in the deep EPL (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior morphological studies

claim: Granule cell soma position correlates with granule cell subtype.
source: GC soma position correlates with GC subtype (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983) and odor-evoked activity in vivo (Wellis and Scott, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Granule cells located in the mitral cell layer and upper granule cell layer tend to exhibit superficial granule cell morphologies and suprathreshold odor responses.
source: Specifically, GCs located in the MCL and upper GCL tend to exhibit sGC morphologies and suprathreshold odor responses while GCs located in the lower GCL tend to exhibit dGC morphologies and subthreshold odor responses (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983; Wellis and Scott, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Granule cells located in the lower granule cell layer tend to exhibit deep granule cell morphologies and subthreshold odor responses.
source: Specifically, GCs located in the MCL and upper GCL tend to exhibit sGC morphologies and suprathreshold odor responses while GCs located in the lower GCL tend to exhibit dGC morphologies and subthreshold odor responses (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983; Wellis and Scott, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Granule cells exhibited distinct superficial or deep morphologies upon visual inspection.
source: Consistent with previous morphological accounts (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983), GCs exhibited distinct sGC or dGC morphologies upon visual inspection (Figure 4a,d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 4

claim: Superficial granule cells preferentially innervate the superficial external plexiform layer while deep granule cells preferentially innervate the deep external plexiform layer.
source: Indeed, reconstruction and visual classification of a large subset of recorded GCs and analysis of the spatial distribution of gemmules – the site of reciprocal dendrodendritic synapse formation (Rall et al., 1966) – confirmed that sGCs preferentially innervate the superficial EPL while dGCs preferentially innervate the deep EPL (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on gemmule distributions shown in Figure 4g

claim: Somatic depth significantly but incompletely predicted granule cell subtype.
source: Moreover, somatic depth significantly – but incompletely – predicted GC subtype (Figure 4a,d; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 1), as previously observed (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior research

claim: Unbiased clustering of granule cells by gemmule distributions yielded 3 distinct clusters: deep granule cells, superficial granule cells, and a small group of superficial granule cells with prominent innervation of the deep glomerular layer.
source: Specifically, clustering of GCs by the Euclidean distances among their normalized gemmule distributions (using Ward's method) and application of the gap statistic method yielded 3 distinct clusters: dGCs, sGCs, and a small group of sGCs with prominent innervation of the deep glomerular layer (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of morphological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c

claim: A greater proportion of superficial granule cells than deep granule cells fired in response to activation of a single glomerulus.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, a strikingly higher percentage of sGCs than dGCs fired in response to activation of a single glomerulus (Figure 4b,e,h) due, at least partially, to stronger excitatory synaptic input to sGCs than dGCs (Figure 4i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Superficial granule cells receive stronger excitatory synaptic input than deep granule cells following glomerular activation.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, a strikingly higher percentage of sGCs than dGCs fired in response to activation of a single glomerulus (Figure 4b,e,h) due, at least partially, to stronger excitatory synaptic input to sGCs than dGCs (Figure 4i).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4i

claim: Superficial granule cells have a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold than deep granule cells.
source: Second, examination of GC biophysical properties revealed several intrinsic differences supporting greater recruitment of sGCs than dGCs, including a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold in sGCs (Figure 4l; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 2) and greater intrinsic excitability in sGCs in response to somatic step current injections (Figure 4j,k; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 3), despite equivalent somatodendritic sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 1) and passive membrane properties (Figure 4—source data 1, Table 4) between sGCs and dGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4l

claim: Superficial granule cells have greater intrinsic excitability than deep granule cells in response to somatic step current injections.
source: Second, examination of GC biophysical properties revealed several intrinsic differences supporting greater recruitment of sGCs than dGCs, including a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold in sGCs (Figure 4l; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 2) and greater intrinsic excitability in sGCs in response to somatic step current injections (Figure 4j,k; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 3), despite equivalent somatodendritic sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 1) and passive membrane properties (Figure 4—source data 1, Table 4) between sGCs and dGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4j,k

claim: Superficial and deep granule cells have equivalent somatodendritic sizes.
source: Second, examination of GC biophysical properties revealed several intrinsic differences supporting greater recruitment of sGCs than dGCs, including a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold in sGCs (Figure 4l; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 2) and greater intrinsic excitability in sGCs in response to somatic step current injections (Figure 4j,k; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 3), despite equivalent somatodendritic sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 1) and passive membrane properties (Figure 4—source data 1, Table 4) between sGCs and dGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d

claim: Superficial and deep granule cells have equivalent passive membrane properties.
source: Second, examination of GC biophysical properties revealed several intrinsic differences supporting greater recruitment of sGCs than dGCs, including a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold in sGCs (Figure 4l; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 2) and greater intrinsic excitability in sGCs in response to somatic step current injections (Figure 4j,k; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 3), despite equivalent somatodendritic sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; Figure 4—source data 1, Table 1) and passive membrane properties (Figure 4—source data 1, Table 4) between sGCs and dGCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in source data tables

claim: There is no difference in spontaneous synaptic event frequency between superficial and deep granule cells.
source: Third, analysis of spontaneous synaptic activity revealed no difference in event frequency or amplitude between sGCs and dGCs (Figure 4—source data 1 Table 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in source data tables

claim: There is no difference in spontaneous synaptic event amplitude between superficial and deep granule cells.
source: Third, analysis of spontaneous synaptic activity revealed no difference in event frequency or amplitude between sGCs and dGCs (Figure 4—source data 1 Table 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in source data tables

claim: The mGluR agonist DHPG at 10 µM selectively enhances the excitability of granule cells but not mitral cells.
source: At this concentration, DHPG selectively enhances the excitability of GCs (Heinbockel et al., 2004) but not MCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The effective activity range of lateral inhibition in mitral cells fell from 31 (± 9)–73 (± 10) Hz to 16 (± 12)–49 (± 23) Hz after adding DHPG.
source: The effective activity range of lateral inhibition in MCs (n=6) fell from 31 (± 9)–73 (± 10) Hz to 16 (± 12)–49 (± 23) Hz after adding DHPG (Figure 5a–d), and the lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition were significantly reduced after the addition of DHPG (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition in mitral cells were significantly reduced after the addition of DHPG.
source: The effective activity range of lateral inhibition in MCs (n=6) fell from 31 (± 9)–73 (± 10) Hz to 16 (± 12)–49 (± 23) Hz after adding DHPG (Figure 5a–d), and the lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition were significantly reduced after the addition of DHPG (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5e

claim: Tufted cells discriminated between 32 similar odors significantly better than mitral cells at low odor concentrations (90% accuracy in tufted cells compared to 70% accuracy in mitral cells at 30% of maximum concentration).
source: For the set of 32 odors, TCs significantly outperformed MCs and the control population at low odor concentrations (90% accuracy in TCs compared to 70% accuracy in MCs at 30% of maximum concentration) while MCs significantly outperformed TCs and the control population at high concentrations (73% accuracy in TCs compared to 91% accuracy in MCs at 60% of maximum concentration).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Mitral cells discriminated between 32 similar odors significantly better than tufted cells at high odor concentrations (91% accuracy in mitral cells compared to 73% accuracy in tufted cells at 60% of maximum concentration).
source: For the set of 32 odors, TCs significantly outperformed MCs and the control population at low odor concentrations (90% accuracy in TCs compared to 70% accuracy in MCs at 30% of maximum concentration) while MCs significantly outperformed TCs and the control population at high concentrations (73% accuracy in TCs compared to 91% accuracy in MCs at 60% of maximum concentration).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Populations using subtractive or divisive inhibition performed no better than control populations lacking inhibition across all concentrations in discriminating 32 odors.
source: We found that populations using subtractive or divisive inhibition performed no better than the control population across all concentrations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c

claim: Models containing a combination of mitral cells and tufted cells significantly outperformed models with only mitral cells or only tufted cells at intervening odor concentrations.
source: However, MC-TC models significantly outperformed other models at intervening odor concentrations.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Models containing a combination of mitral cells and tufted cells performed significantly better than models composed of only mitral cells or only tufted cells when averaging discrimination accuracy across all concentrations tested.
source: Interestingly, MC-TC models also exhibited the second best performance at high and low concentrations, and after averaging discrimination accuracy across all concentrations tested, we found that models containing a combination of MCs and TCs performed significantly better than models composed of only MCs or only TCs (Figure 6m).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6m

claim: Differences in activity-dependent lateral inhibition between mitral and tufted cells likely reflect differences in the activation of deep and superficial granule cells.
source: We find differences in activity-dependent lateral inhibition between mitral and tufted cells that likely reflect newly described differences in the activation of deep and superficial granule cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on granule cell subtypes and their differential recruitment

claim: Circuit-level differences between mitral and tufted cells allow them to best discriminate odors in separate concentration ranges.
source: Simulations show that these circuit-level differences allow mitral and tufted cells to best discriminate odors in separate concentration ranges, indicating that segregating information about different ranges of stimulus intensity may be an important function of these parallel sensory pathways.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results

claim: Segregating information about different ranges of stimulus intensity may be an important function of the parallel sensory pathways formed by mitral and tufted cells.
source: Simulations show that these circuit-level differences allow mitral and tufted cells to best discriminate odors in separate concentration ranges, indicating that segregating information about different ranges of stimulus intensity may be an important function of these parallel sensory pathways.
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling results

claim: Motion and color are segregated in the visual system.
source: Motion and color are segregated in the visual system (Merigan and Maunsell, 1993; Callaway, 2005), sound location and tonal pattern are processed in parallel pathways in the auditory system (Lomber and Malhotra, 2008), and pain and itch are conveyed by distinct pathways in the somatosensory system (Davidson and Giesler, 2010; Ross, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Sound location and tonal pattern are processed in parallel pathways in the auditory system.
source: Motion and color are segregated in the visual system (Merigan and Maunsell, 1993; Callaway, 2005), sound location and tonal pattern are processed in parallel pathways in the auditory system (Lomber and Malhotra, 2008), and pain and itch are conveyed by distinct pathways in the somatosensory system (Davidson and Giesler, 2010; Ross, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Pain and itch are conveyed by distinct pathways in the somatosensory system.
source: Motion and color are segregated in the visual system (Merigan and Maunsell, 1993; Callaway, 2005), sound location and tonal pattern are processed in parallel pathways in the auditory system (Lomber and Malhotra, 2008), and pain and itch are conveyed by distinct pathways in the somatosensory system (Davidson and Giesler, 2010; Ross, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Firing of olfactory sensory neurons excites two classes of projection neurons – mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: In the mammalian olfactory bulb, firing of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) excites two classes of projection neurons – mitral cells and tufted cells (MCs and TCs).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of olfactory bulb circuitry

claim: Tufted cells are involved in processing near-threshold stimuli.
source: For instance, TCs respond to lower odor concentrations than MCs (Igarashi et al., 2012; Kikuta et al., 2013), suggesting that TCs are involved in processing near-threshold stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from citations showing TCs respond to lower concentrations

claim: Higher firing rates in M72 tufted cells alone is insufficient to explain the differences in both the lower and upper bound in the effective activity range of lateral inhibition between mitral cells and tufted cells.
source: Given that TCs fire at higher rates than MCs following glomerular activation (Burton and Urban, 2014), M72 TCs will fire at higher rates than M72 MCs following M72 photoactivation and, in part, contribute to the decreased lower bound of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition in postsynaptic TCs. However, higher firing rates in M72 TCs alone is insufficient to explain the differences in both the lower and upper bound in the effective activity range of lateral inhibition between MCs and TCs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and logical reasoning

claim: Preferential connectivity of tufted cells with superficial granule cells and mitral cells with deep granule cells can explain the observed differences in the activity-dependence of lateral inhibition.
source: While preferential connectivity of TCs with sGCs and MCs with dGCs can explain the observed differences in the activity-dependence of lateral inhibition, other circuit mechanisms may also contribute.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on granule cell subtypes and their properties

claim: External plexiform layer interneurons can mediate inhibition onto mitral/tufted cells.
source: In particular, EPL interneurons (EPL-INs) can mediate inhibition onto M/TCs (Huang et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2013; Miyamichi et al., 2013), and it remains possible that EPL-INs or distinct subclasses of EPL-INs preferentially inhibit MCs or TCs.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: External plexiform layer interneurons mediate linear (divisive) but not activity-dependent inhibition of mitral/tufted cell outputs.
source: However, it is unlikely that EPL-INs predominantly drive the difference in MC vs. TC ADLI given that EPL-INs mediate linear (divisive) but not activity-dependent inhibition of MC/TC outputs (Kato et al., 2013; Uchida et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Glomerular layer circuits play a role in mitral/tufted cell lateral inhibition.
source: Glomerular layer circuits have also been shown to play a role in M/TC lateral inhibition (Aungst et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2013; Whitesell et al., 2013; Banerjee et al., 2015), however these circuits likely do not play a role in the differences in ADLI reported here because our results were not influenced by apical dendrite truncation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Glomerular layer circuits likely do not play a role in the differences in activity-dependent lateral inhibition between mitral and tufted cells because results were not influenced by apical dendrite truncation.
source: Glomerular layer circuits have also been shown to play a role in M/TC lateral inhibition (Aungst et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2013; Whitesell et al., 2013; Banerjee et al., 2015), however these circuits likely do not play a role in the differences in ADLI reported here because our results were not influenced by apical dendrite truncation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on cells with intact vs. truncated apical dendrites

claim: Granule cells form two distinct morphological subclasses – superficial granule cells and deep granule cells – rather than a continuum of morphologies.
source: Here, we provide quantitative evidence that GCs indeed form two distinct morphological subclasses – sGCs and dGCs – rather than a continuum of morphologies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on granule cell morphologies and clustering analysis

claim: Weaker lateral inhibitory currents may contribute to the finding that tufted cells are less frequently inhibited by odors.
source: Our data describe local, circuit-level mechanisms that can account for several differences between MC and TC odor-evoked responses observed in vivo. Weaker lateral inhibitory currents may contribute to the finding that TCs are less frequently inhibited by odors (Nagayama et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited in vivo observations

claim: The finding that intermediate and high firing rates are unaffected by lateral inhibition in tufted cells may help explain why tufted cells show odor-evoked responses that are more highly correlated to olfactory sensory neuron input.
source: Additionally, the finding that intermediate and high firing rates are unaffected by lateral inhibition in TCs may help explain why TCs show odor-evoked responses that are more highly correlated to OSN input (Adam et al., 2014) and less dependent on concentration (Fukunaga et al., 2012; Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited in vivo observations

claim: The finding that intermediate and high firing rates are unaffected by lateral inhibition in tufted cells may help explain why tufted cells show odor-evoked responses that are less dependent on concentration.
source: Additionally, the finding that intermediate and high firing rates are unaffected by lateral inhibition in TCs may help explain why TCs show odor-evoked responses that are more highly correlated to OSN input (Adam et al., 2014) and less dependent on concentration (Fukunaga et al., 2012; Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited in vivo observations

claim: Tufted cells firing above the upper bound of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition are shielded from granule cell-mediated inhibition triggered by cortical feedback.
source: Additionally, TCs firing above the upper bound of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition are shielded, not only from lateral inhibition, but other sources of GC-mediated inhibition as well, such as inhibition triggered by cortical feedback (Boyd et al., 2012; Markopoulos et al., 2012), Consequently, the circuit-level differences we describe may explain why MCs but not TCs are decorrelated by cortical feedback (Otazu et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited research on cortical feedback

claim: The circuit-level differences between mitral and tufted cells may explain why mitral cells but not tufted cells are decorrelated by cortical feedback.
source: Additionally, TCs firing above the upper bound of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition are shielded, not only from lateral inhibition, but other sources of GC-mediated inhibition as well, such as inhibition triggered by cortical feedback (Boyd et al., 2012; Markopoulos et al., 2012), Consequently, the circuit-level differences we describe may explain why MCs but not TCs are decorrelated by cortical feedback (Otazu et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited research on cortical feedback

claim: Activity in mitral/tufted cell populations becomes decorrelated over time.
source: Prior work has shown that activity in M/TC populations becomes decorrelated over time (Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010) and that this decorrelation is driven by GCs (Gschwend et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Decorrelation of mitral/tufted cell activity is driven by granule cells.
source: Prior work has shown that activity in M/TC populations becomes decorrelated over time (Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010) and that this decorrelation is driven by GCs (Gschwend et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Granule cell-mediated mitral/tufted cell decorrelation improves odor discrimination.
source: Additionally, GC-mediated M/TC decorrelation improves odor discrimination (Gschwend et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Activity-dependent lateral inhibition likely improves odor discrimination by driving decorrelation of mitral/tufted cell firing in ranges that engage lateral inhibition.
source: Consequently, ADLI likely improves odor discrimination by driving decorrelation of M/TC firing in ranges that engage lateral inhibition (Arevian et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from prior research on decorrelation and discrimination

claim: In the retina, rods and cones function best at different ranges of light intensity.
source: For instance, rods and cones in the retina function best at different ranges of light intensity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of retinal physiology

claim: In the retina, feature selectivity in each ganglion cell type emerges due to its connectivity to specific bipolar and amacrine cell types.
source: In the retina, feature selectivity in each ganglion cell type emerges due to its connectivity to specific bipolar and amacrine cell types (Masland, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Differences in odor-evoked responses in mitral cells and tufted cells emerge due to differences in connectivity to olfactory sensory neurons, external tufted cells, and granule cells.
source: Similarly, differences in odor-evoked responses in MCs and TCs emerge due to differences in connectivity to OSNs, external tufted cells (Najac et al., 2011; Gire et al., 2012) and GCs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited research

claim: If populations of neurons in higher order sensory areas integrate inputs from parallel sensory channels and perform simple computations such as averaging, new features may emerge.
